teaser: She could not stand like this in real life. Botticelli knew, and painted her anyway.

lesson.text: Start in the hills a few miles north of Florence, at a country house called the Villa di Castello. It belonged to a young cousin of the Medici, the family that ran the city. Around 1550 the writer Giorgio Vasari visited and described a Venus “being born” hanging on its walls. That is the first time anyone mentions this picture.

Nobody can prove it was painted for that house, but the object itself points to the countryside. Botticelli worked on canvas, at a time when serious Florentine pictures were made on heavy wooden panels. Canvas was lighter, cheaper and a little informal. It suited a villa, a place for summer, poetry and guests.

And it is big: about 172 by 278 cm (roughly 5 ft 8 in by 9 ft 2 in). In a villa room the goddess would have stood nearly as tall as the people looking at her. The subject comes from ancient myth. Venus, goddess of love, is born fully grown from the foam of the sea and drifts to land.

So the title is slightly off. Nobody is being born here. She has already risen from the water, and what Botticelli shows is the landing. Three groups share the work: someone pushes, someone arrives, someone waits on the shore.

lesson.title: Push, arrive, receive
lesson.text: Follow the action from left to right, the way the wind blows.

spots.title: The winds
spots.text: Zephyr, the west wind, flies with a female companion locked around him. Their cheeks are puffed. Their breath is what moves the shell, and it scatters pink roses across the sky.

spots.title: Venus
spots.text: Her head tilts, her eyes drift past you. Her hair streams to the right, the only part of her that admits there is any wind at all.

spots.title: The welcome
spots.text: A young woman, usually read as a goddess of spring, runs up on tiptoe with a pink cloak sewn with flowers. In a second Venus will be covered. You are seeing her just before.

lesson.text: The cloak matters. For a Florentine of the 1480s, a life-size naked woman who was not Eve in a Bible story was a startling thing to put on a wall. Almost nothing like it had been painted since ancient Rome, a thousand years earlier.

Botticelli borrowed her pose from ancient statues known as the Venus Pudica, the “modest Venus,” who covers herself with her hands. Then he bent the rules of the body. Her neck is too long. One shoulder slides down far too steeply. And her weight sits where no leg could hold it.
Three lines show how the picture is built, and why Venus seems to float rather than stand.

lines.label: A long S
lines.text: Her body sways in one curve from head to foot, and both feet crowd the front lip of the shell. A real woman in this pose would tip forward into the sea.

lines.label: The gust
lines.text: The two winds form one long slant that leans in toward her. It aims the whole left side of the canvas at the goddess.

lines.label: The cloak
lines.text: On the right the arm and the billowing cloth lean in the opposite way. Together the two slants make a roof over Venus and hold her in the center.

lesson.text: Botticelli was not after anatomy. He stretched and tilted the body until it became a line, and that line is what makes Venus look weightless.

The paint helps. This is tempera, colored powder mixed with egg yolk, which dries fast and stays pale and matte. There are almost no deep shadows. The sea is a flat green sheet marked with small white V shapes, more like a pattern on cloth than real water.
Botticelli finished the canvas with real gold. Fine gold lines glint in Venus's hair, on the wings of the winds, along the ribs of the shell and on the trunks and leaves of the trees.
The trees on the right are orange trees, and the shore is strewn with details a visitor to the villa could enjoy slowly. One of them is out of place on a seashore, and it is easy to miss.
Some plants here belong beside a pond or a river, not in salt water. Can you spot them?

spots.title: The cattails
spots.text: Tall golden cattails rise from the corner. They grow in fresh water, never in the sea. Botticelli wanted their upright shapes to anchor the corner and did not mind the botany.

lesson.text: Old Florentine gossip adds a face to the story. Legend says Venus has the features of Simonetta Vespucci, a celebrated beauty who died young in 1476, about a decade before this was painted. There is no proof. What is certain is that Botticelli was buried in the church of Ognissanti, where her family had its tombs.
If you have ever paid with Italian coins, you may have carried her in your pocket. The head of Botticelli's Venus is stamped on Italy's 10 cent euro coin.

quiz.question: Where is the painting first recorded?
options: In a Medici country villa near Florence
quiz.explanation: Vasari described it at the Villa di Castello around 1550.

quiz.question: What is unusual about its support for Florence in the 1480s?
quiz.explanation: Most important Florentine pictures were on wooden panels, this one is on canvas.

quiz.question: Which moment of the myth does Botticelli actually show?
quiz.explanation: She is already born and is being blown to land.

quiz.question: Why would a real woman fall over in Venus's pose?
options: Her weight sits where no leg could support it
She is standing on one toe
quiz.explanation: Her body sways in an S and her feet crowd the edge of the shell.

quiz.question: Which plants in the picture do not belong in the sea?
quiz.explanation: Cattails grow in fresh water, yet they rise from the corner of the sea.

facts.text: Botticelli used real gold for highlights in the painting.
facts.explanation: Gold lines glint in the hair, the wings, the shell and the trees.

facts.text: The painting is made with oil paint on a wooden panel.
facts.explanation: It is tempera, pigment mixed with egg yolk, on canvas.

facts.text: The pose of Venus comes from ancient statues called the Venus Pudica.
facts.explanation: The “modest Venus” covers herself with her hands, as she does here.
